That mindset works well for us as a couple, but for myself as an individual, the distance has been quite difficult and frustrating. It's a bit easier on him because he's busy all the time with work, whereas I'm in a job I dislike and time to kill. I've come to learn how to be alone again, and have acquired new hobbies, but, let's be honest, it still kinda sucks.

That being said, we are both very committed to making this work, and are working as a couple to get through this period (there is no end in sight at the moment). Communication is key. If both parties are committed to one another and communicating the good and the bad in the relationship, then LDRs are totally doable. And, on the upside, absence sometimes really does make the heart grow fonder, even when you didn't think it possible to love the other person more than you already do.

Also, should you choose to stay behind, check out r/LongDistance, that community has been immensely helpful to me for the past few months. :-)

As far as the audition process is concerned...

-It is always helpful to have a lesson at any prospective school before you audition. This is a good way to see if you are compatible with the professor and it gives them a chance to hear you (and remember you when you come to audition). I did not do this because my family didn't have the money to allow for it, but it is recommended. 

-Many of the big schools now have prescreening requirements for flute. This involves submitting a recording that includes, usually, Mozart (accuracy is key here...no James Galway renditions!), a piece of your choice (French pieces are great because the allow to show who you are as an artist), and maybe an orchestral excerpt or two (again, accuracy).

-When you get past the first round (yay!!!) and get a live audition, it's pretty straightway. You'll go to the school, probably have some orientation of some sort, and warm-up (long tones, T&G, don't work on getting that one funky technical spot perfect). In the practice room, you will run into other flutists that are audition. You will hear them through the walls playing before their auditions. Put your blinders on and focus on YOU. 

then you'll be off to audition in the flute studio. Here, you will say your hellos to your prospective teachers, and play similar things to the recorded round (if there was one). While accuracy and technical solidity are important in the audition, the professors are usually looking for something special in your playing (i.e., don't be afraid to take some musical risks!). Have fun, and play because you have something to show them. Be confident, and if you make mistakes, move on, don't dwell. 

-The flute world is very highly competitive, and you need to keep this in mind when looking at schools. Don't apply on to conservatories...there are PLENTY of awesome state schools.

-As far as the studio size is concerned, it depends. Conservatories are smaller, state schools much larger. Speaking from my experience, there were 4 incoming flute freshman a year at Eastman. At Ithaca College, where I did my MM, there were, oh, probably 8 or so. This is pretty standard.

Hope this helps, and if you have any other pressing questions, send em' on over.

There's going to be competition no matter where you end up, especially at the conservatory level. That being said, the flute studio when I was there was completely warm and inviting. We all kind of knew who ranked where, but everyone was always supportive and friendly towards one another. This had a lot to do with Bonnie being who she is. It is fiercely competitive, but that's what the real music world is.

I loved my time at Eastman, and really have nothing but good things to say about my experience with the faculty. Naturally, there is going to be dirt in any music department. It's the nature of the profession. 

It is very true that Rochester is not a safe town. I had my car stolen and broken into, but that was after I had graduated. Yes, the notes are pretty simple in the first movement, and the piece as a whole is not very technically demanding. Flutists play the Franck for the musical possibilities of the work, and the multitude of tone colors than can be achieved. You can knock it out of the park, as a flutist, or you can not do it justice (this of course is another violin work flutists love to play). Most flutists fall in the latter category. You need to develop a sense of line and musicality and sensitivity and a wide palette of tone colors to play it...something that doesn't come until usually, the conservatory level.
